blocks.text: A cultural detail that clarifies the passage is this: Matthew cannot legitimately be used to excuse abuse, stigmatize disability or mental illness, enforce misogyny or anti-LGBTQ harm, blame poverty, set apocalyptic dates, or map ancient judgments onto modern peoples.
A cultural detail that clarifies the passage is this: Beasts, numbers, and cosmic imagery were common ways to speak about empires and divine sovereignty.

A cultural detail that clarifies the passage is this: Ancient background for Glorification includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Daniel 7:13-14, Daniel 12:1-3, eschatology, and second-coming without letting comparison replace the biblical witness. Ancient background for Eschatology includes covenant life, temple worship, royal ideology, wisdom teaching, and early church confession; the entry ties that world to Daniel 7:13-14, Daniel 12:1-3, second-coming, and final-judgment without letting comparison replace the biblical witness. Historically, this chapter is read within the following setting: Apocalyptic writing emerges in pressure, exile, and persecution as faithful communities ask how God will act.

This helps frame an interpretive question raised by the passage: Many scholars date Matthew approximately 70-100 CE, often after Jerusalem's temple destruction, but no exact year is textually stated. Matthew 24-25 combines temple destruction, tribulation, Son of Man coming, uncertainty of timing, readiness, stewardship, and judgment. This helps frame an interpretive question raised by the passage: The Synoptic Gospels and Revelation reuse Danielic abomination, distress, humanlike-figure, beast, horn, time, saint, book, and judgment imagery in new literary settings. The desolating abomination has an Antiochene temple-desecration horizon and later Jewish and Christian reuses; each reuse must be identified rather than collapsed.
